records.answer:
On Thursday 5 November 2026, **419 of 461 Halifax Transit blocks (90.9%)** could run on one overnight charge using summer energy figures. The other **42 blocks** drive farther than one charge allows.

**How this was worked out**
- **Range per charge: 233.6 km.** That is a 400 kWh battery, of which 71.25% (285 kWh) is usable, divided by 1.22 kWh per km. All three numbers are **sourced** from *TTC's Green Bus Program: Final Results of TTC's Head-to-Head eBus Evaluation*, Toronto Transit Commission, p. 55: https://www.ttc.ca/All-public-meetings/board/2022/Board-Meeting-Apr-14
- It assumes the bus charges once overnight and not during the day.
- It counts only km driven with passengers. Empty trips to and from the garage aren't included, so the real picture is somewhat worse than this.

**Longest blocks that day**
| Block | km |
|---|---|
| 722134 | 457.5 |
| 722151 | 364.8 |
| 722165 | 363.5 |
| 722252 | 363.2 |
| 712134 | 363.0 |

Block 722134 needs nearly twice the range of one charge.

**Data used:** Halifax Transit timetable feed `halifax.zip`, version 2026_08_August_20260806, which covers 24 August to 29 November 2026. Distances are exact, taken from the timetable's own distance data, and blocks are as the feed publishes them. Nothing is estimated or inferred.

**Caveat:** You asked for summer figures, but early November in Halifax will often need heating, which uses more energy. The tool's winter setting assumes 1.425 times the energy per km, so fewer blocks would fit on one charge. I can run the same date with winter figures if you'd like to compare.

**Halifax Transit should plan its winter electric fleet around Monday, 24 August 2026. On that day, 130 of its 461 blocks would be too long for one charge.**

**The design day**
- 24 August 2026 has the most blocks over one charge's range of any day in the timetable. When days tie on that, the rule picks the day with the most blocks in service, then the earliest date.
- Nine other dates have exactly the same block pattern, including 25–28 August, 31 August, 1–2 September, 25 September and 23 October. A plan that works for 24 August covers all of them.
- **About the dates:** the timetable only runs from 24 August to 29 November 2026, so the hardest day falls in late summer. "Winter" here means the timetable's hardest day with winter energy use applied. A real winter timetable might be different and should be checked once it's published.

**Results for that day (winter)**
- Range on one charge: **163.9 km**
- Blocks within range: **331 (71.8%)**
- Blocks too long for one charge: **130**
- Longest blocks: 722134 (457.5 km), 722151 (364.8 km), 722165 (363.5 km), 722252 (363.2 km) and 712134 (363.0 km). The longest block is almost three times the range.

**How the range is worked out (all sourced)**
- Battery: 400 kWh nominal, of which 71.25% is usable, giving 285 kWh. Source: TTC, *TTC's Green Bus Program: Final Results of TTC's Head-to-Head eBus Evaluation*, p. 55, https://www.ttc.ca/All-public-meetings/board/2022/Board-Meeting-Apr-14
- Winter energy use: 1.7385 kWh/km. This is TTC's summer figure of 1.22 kWh/km raised by 42.5%, the middle of a Finnish study's finding that winter use is 40–45% higher. Source: Vehviläinen et al., *Setting Up and Operating Electric City Buses in Harsh Winter Conditions*, Applied Sciences 12(6) 2762, 2022, p. 1, https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/12/6/2762. TTC's own winter figure wasn't used because its test buses also burned diesel for heating.

**Limits of this check**
- It assumes each bus charges once overnight and not during the day.
- It only counts km driven in passenger service. Empty running to and from the garage is left out, so the real number of blocks that are too long is probably a bit higher than 130.

**Data:** Halifax feed version 2026_08_August_20260806 (sha256 f5d95091c813). Distances are exact, taken from the feed's own measurements (not estimated), and blocks are the feed's published block IDs (not inferred).

On a winter design day, Halifax Transit would need **about 414 electric buses, compared with 284 buses today**. That is a **replacement ratio of about 1.46**.

| | Buses |
|---|---|
| Buses needed today (most blocks running at the same moment) | 284 |
| Blocks running on the design day | 461 |
| Blocks too long for one winter charge (163.9 km) | 130 |
| **Electric buses needed** | **414** |
| **Replacement ratio** (electric buses ÷ buses today) | **1.458** |
| Benchmark ratio, for comparison | 1.2 |

Halifax's ratio is well above the 1.2 benchmark. The main reason is winter range: 130 of the 461 blocks (about 28%) drive farther than one full charge would cover.

**How it was worked out (a rough estimate):**
- **Design day:** the timetable day with the most blocks over range is 24 August 2026. The timetable only runs from 24 August to 29 November 2026, so this is a summer date with winter energy use applied as a "what if."
- **Buses today:** the largest number of blocks in service at the same moment on that day.
- **Electric buses:** today's buses plus one extra bus for each block over range. This assumes a freshly charged bus takes over partway through the day.
- **Not included:** spare buses, so the real number would be higher.
- **Charging:** buses charge once overnight, with no charging during the day.
- **Distance:** only the kilometres driven with passengers count, not empty trips to and from the garage. That makes the estimate optimistic.

**Range assumptions:**
- **Battery:** 400 kWh, of which 71.25% (285 kWh) is usable, as measured in service. Source: Toronto Transit Commission, *TTC's Green Bus Program: Final Results of TTC's Head-to-Head eBus Evaluation*, p. 55. https://www.ttc.ca/All-public-meetings/board/2022/Board-Meeting-Apr-14
- **Winter energy use:** 1.7385 kWh per km. This is TTC's summer figure of 1.22 kWh/km × 1.425, the middle of a Finnish finding that buses use 40–45% more energy in winter. Source: Vehviläinen et al., *Setting Up and Operating Electric City Buses in Harsh Winter Conditions*, Applied Sciences 12(6) 2762, 2022, p. 1. https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/12/6/2762
  - TTC's own winter figure (1.40 kWh/km) wasn't used, because its test buses also burned diesel for heating.
- **The 1.2 benchmark is a placeholder:** it's a commonly quoted planning figure, not taken from a cited source.

**Data:** the figures come from Halifax Transit timetable feed version 2026_08_August_20260806 (sha256 f5d95091c813). Distances are exact, taken from the feed, and blocks are the ones the feed publishes, so none of these figures are estimated or inferred.

records.answer:
On the hardest service day in the timetable, Halifax Transit's electric fleet would need about **92 MWh of energy overnight in winter**. If every bus charged at once over a 6-hour window, the depot would need a **peak of about 15.4 MW**. Both numbers are rough estimates, and the real need is likely higher.

**Results**
| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Hardest day used | 2026-08-24 |
| Blocks in service | 461 |
| Total distance that day | 52,983 km |
| **Overnight energy** | **92,111 kWh (≈ 92.1 MWh)** |
| Charging window | 6 hours (a placeholder, see below) |
| **Peak depot power** | **15,352 kW (≈ 15.4 MW)** |

**How the tool worked it out**
- **Energy:** each block's km on that day, added up, times 1.7385 kWh per km (winter energy use).
- **Power:** that energy spread evenly over the charging window, assuming every bus charges at the same time.
- The hardest day falls in August because the timetable runs from 24 August to 29 November 2026. The winter energy rate was applied to that day's distances. This shows what that service level would need under winter conditions.

**Assumptions and sources**
- **Winter energy use, 1.7385 kWh/km (sourced):** a summer figure of 1.22 kWh/km from Toronto's TTC, raised by 42.5%. That uplift is the midpoint of a Finnish study finding winter use is 40–45% higher than summer: Vehviläinen et al., *Setting Up and Operating Electric City Buses in Harsh Winter Conditions*, Applied Sciences 12(6) 2762, 2022, p. 1, https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/12/6/2762. TTC's own measured winter figure (1.40 kWh/km) wasn't used because its test buses also burned diesel for heating.
- **Battery, 400 kWh with 285 kWh usable (sourced):** TTC, *TTC's Green Bus Program: Final Results of TTC's Head-to-Head eBus Evaluation*, p. 55, https://www.ttc.ca/All-public-meetings/board/2022/Board-Meeting-Apr-14.
- **6-hour charging window (placeholder):** this is not a sourced figure. The peak power depends directly on it: a longer window means a lower peak, and a shorter one a higher peak.

**Why the real need is probably higher**
- **Passenger trips only:** the distances leave out empty trips to and from the garage, so actual energy use will be higher.
- **Everyone charging at once:** the peak assumes all buses charge at the same time. Staggered or managed charging could lower it. The figure also ignores charger efficiency losses.
- **Some blocks are too long for one charge:** their full energy is still counted, but in practice those buses would need daytime charging or a second bus.

**Data:** the figures come from Halifax Transit's GTFS timetable feed, version `2026_08_August_20260806` (sha256 f5d95091c813). Block distances are exact, taken from the feed's own distance data rather than estimated. The blocks are the ones published in the feed, not inferred.

records.answer:
Electrifying Halifax Transit would cost about **CAD 654 million** up front. It would save about **19,400 tonnes of CO2 a year** and about **CAD 8.3 million a year** in energy costs, assuming winter energy use all year. These are rough figures.

**What the model found**
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Electric buses needed | 414 (130 more than today's fleet) |
| Chargers | 414 (one per bus, included in the bus price) |
| **Capital cost** | **CAD 653.7 million** |
| Distance per year | 15.9 million km |
| Electricity per year | CAD 4.14 million |
| Diesel per year (today) | CAD 12.43 million |
| **Energy saving per year** | **CAD 8.28 million** |
| **CO2 saved per year** | **19,449 tonnes** |

At that saving, the capital cost would take about 79 years to pay back. That number is misleading, though: the cost counts every bus, including buses that would have to be replaced with new diesels anyway. The fair comparison is the extra cost over new diesel buses, which the tool doesn't calculate.

**How it was worked out**
- **Number of buses:** one electric bus for each bus in service today on the busiest day, plus one more for each block that's too long for one charge. A block is the day's work for one bus. The busiest day is the timetable's hardest day for electric buses (pattern starting 24 Aug 2026). Spare buses aren't included.
- **Capital cost:** number of buses × Halifax's price per bus, which includes the charger. Grid upgrades aren't included.
- **Distance per year:** the busiest day's distance × 300 service days.
- **CO2 saved:** litres of diesel no longer burned × kg of CO2 per litre. Emissions from making the electricity are not subtracted, so the saving is too high. How high depends on Nova Scotia's power mix.
- **Optimistic in places:** distances count only trips carrying passengers, not driving to and from the garage. The model also assumes one overnight charge and no charging during the day.

**Sourced figures**
- **Bus price:** CAD 1,578,998 per bus, including its charger ($94.7M for 60 buses). From *Award – RFP 21-021*, Halifax Regional Council, 17 May 2022, p. 2, https://www.halifax.ca/media/77822
- **Winter energy use:** 1.7385 kWh/km, which is the Toronto summer figure of 1.22 raised by 42.5% for winter. The uplift is from *Setting Up and Operating Electric City Buses in Harsh Winter Conditions*, Vehviläinen et al., Applied Sciences 2022, p. 1, https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/12/6/2762
- **Battery:** 400 kWh, of which 285 kWh is usable. From *TTC's Green Bus Program: Final Results*, Toronto Transit Commission, p. 55, https://www.ttc.ca/All-public-meetings/board/2022/Board-Meeting-Apr-14
- **One charger per bus:** *Financial Analysis of Battery Electric Transit Buses*, NREL 2020, p. 15, https://afdc.energy.gov/files/u/publication/financial_analysis_be_transit_buses.pdf
- **Diesel use:** 0.46 L/km, which is an Irish city bus fleet figure, not a Halifax one. From *Report on Diesel and Alternative-Fuel Bus Trials*, Irish Department of Transport, 2019, p. 24, https://www.gov.ie/en/publication/7251e2-low-emission-bus-trials-report/
- **Diesel CO2:** 2.66 kg per litre. From *Fuel consumption and CO2 (AutoSmart factsheet 6)*, Natural Resources Canada, p. 2, https://www.nrcan.gc.ca/sites/www.nrcan.gc.ca/files/oee/pdf/transportation/fuel-efficient-technologies/autosmart_factsheet_6_e.pdf

**Placeholders (not from any source, so the energy saving is only indicative)**
- Electricity price: CAD 0.15/kWh
- Diesel price: CAD 1.70/L
- Service days per year: 300

**Data used:** Halifax Transit timetable version 2026_08_August_20260806, covering 24 Aug to 29 Nov 2026. Distances come exactly from the timetable data, not estimates. Blocks are the ones Halifax publishes, not inferred. The busiest day falls in August, but winter energy use is applied to the whole year, as you asked. That's conservative for electricity cost and range, and it's the main reason 130 extra buses are needed.

records.answer:
Natural Resources Canada says burning one litre of diesel releases **2.66 kg of CO2** at the tailpipe.

The same factsheet gives figures for some other fuels:
- B5 biodiesel blend: 2.65 kg CO2 per litre
- B20 biodiesel blend: 2.62 kg CO2 per litre
- Gasoline: 2.29 kg CO2 per litre

**Source:** Natural Resources Canada, *Learn the facts: Fuel consumption and CO2* (AutoSmart factsheet 6), 2014, p. 2. https://www.nrcan.gc.ca/sites/www.nrcan.gc.ca/files/oee/pdf/transportation/fuel-efficient-technologies/autosmart_factsheet_6_e.pdf

This counts only CO2 from the tailpipe. It leaves out emissions from producing and transporting the fuel.

records.answer:
I can't answer that with the tools I have. They cover timetable data (how far each bus block drives and how long it's in service) and electric-bus planning (range, fleet size, charging, cost and CO2). None of them include ridership or passenger loads. The public sources I can search are about electric-bus energy use, prices, charging and fleet plans, not passenger counts. I won't guess a number.

**Where to find it:**
- **Halifax Transit / Halifax Regional Municipality reports:** Ridership and load figures sometimes appear in Transit reports to Regional Council, Moving Forward Together Plan updates and annual budget documents.
- **Halifax Open Data portal:** Check for ridership or automatic passenger counter (APC) datasets.
- **Ask Halifax Transit directly:** Peak-hour load data usually comes from APC systems and may be available on request.

**What I can help with:**
- How many buses are on the road at the busiest time of the design day (the hardest service day in the timetable), and how many electric buses would be needed
- How far a given block drives, or how long it's in service during the rush-hour period
- Whether the fleet's blocks could run on one battery charge in summer or winter
- Overnight charging energy, depot power, cost and CO2 estimates

I can't answer that with what I have. My tools cover timetables, battery range, charging, bus and charger prices, energy costs and CO2. None of them has wage or labour-cost data, and the public documents I can search don't cover pay either. I won't guess a figure.

**Where to find it:**
- **The union contract:** Halifax Transit operators are covered by a collective agreement with ATU Local 508. The agreement lists hourly rates, including the steps of the pay scale.
- **The Halifax Regional Municipality:** HRM job postings for transit operators and its budget documents usually give the current starting and top hourly rates.

**What I can help with:** questions about switching to battery-electric buses. For example:
- Whether specific blocks could run on one overnight charge
- How many electric buses would be needed compared with today's fleet
- How much depot charging power would be needed
- Rough capital and energy costs, and CO2 savings

My cost figures don't include driver labour. Extra buses would probably mean extra driver hours, so if you get the wage rate from one of the sources above, you could weigh it alongside the fleet-size results.
